results.summary: This is a first Wokwi project by Matt, described only as 'Mi primer proyecto' with placeholder documentation. The how-it-works, how-to-test and external-hardware sections all contain the word 'explicado' rather than real content. No pins, clock or behaviour are specified, so nothing concrete can be said about what the design does. It appears to be a beginner exercise rather than a documented design.

The project is titled Tiny Tapeout JMCG and its one-line description is simply 'LSFR', indicating a linear-feedback shift register. The documentation sections are all left as the default placeholder text, so the polynomial, width and reset behaviour are not stated. No pins, external hardware or test procedure are described. It is a minimal Wokwi design whose only concrete information is the LFSR intent and a 10 MHz clock.

This project is described as a flip-flop example driving a seven-segment display. The documentation body is entirely placeholder text, so the flip-flop type, clocking and display mapping are not specified. No pins, clock frequency or external hardware are given beyond the title. It appears to be a teaching example, but the lack of detail means the exact behaviour cannot be confirmed.

All documentation fields still contain the default 'Explain how your project works' placeholder text. No pins, clock or behaviour are described, so the design's function is unknown. It appears to be a workshop exercise rather than a documented project.

This project is a 4-bit linear-feedback shift register with reset, created for the Tiny Tapeout Workshop in Malaga. The documentation sections are placeholder text, so the feedback taps and reset polarity are not documented. A 10 MHz clock is specified, but no pins or external hardware are listed. The only concrete information is the 4-bit LFSR with reset intent.

This is an 8-bit MIPS-inspired single-cycle processor with eight registers, an ALU, branches and jumps, scaled to fit one Tiny Tapeout tile. It runs a hardcoded program automatically after reset; three input pins select which register is shown on the eight outputs, while five bidirectional pins expose the program counter and one shows a halt flag. Testing needs only LEDs on the outputs and switches on the register-select inputs, with no external hardware required. It is notable for preserving core MIPS concepts in a very small area, though the documentation does not report silicon results.

Matt's first Wokwi design is described only as 'It shows 1 to 4'. The how-it-works, how-to-test and external-hardware sections all contain placeholder text. No pins, clock or output format are specified, so it is unclear whether the numbers appear on a display, LEDs or something else. The design is essentially undocumented beyond its title and one-line description.

This project is a basic logic-gate circuit built from the Tiny Tapeout template, described as a flip-flop. The documentation fields are all placeholder text, so the gate arrangement and flip-flop behaviour are not described. A 10 kHz clock is specified, but no pins or external hardware are listed. It appears to be a simple educational exercise with no further detail available.

This first Wokwi design maps eight input switches to eight outputs labelled as display lines. The documentation body is placeholder text, so the mapping between switches and display segments or digits is not explained. Pin names indicate switches on ui[0..7] and display outputs on uo[0..7], but no clock or external hardware is specified. It is a beginner exercise whose exact function cannot be confirmed from the documentation.
